tldr: This paper presents Dogger, a modular quadruped robot that allows flexible reconfiguration of leg segment lengths and passive knee spring compliance. Using a two-stage framework combining reinforcement learning and Bayesian optimization, task-optimized hardware and controllers were deployed zero-shot from simulation to hardware, achieving substantial energy savings with cost of transport reductions of up to 35.7%.
hero_caption: Overall view of the proposed two-stage co-design framework. In simulation, a universal control policy conditioned on morphology parameters is trained via reinforcement learning. With this policy held fixed, Bayesian optimization selects the task-specific optimal hardware. The selected design is then directly applied to the physical robot, operating immediately without additional training.
overview:
In quadruped robot design, the conventional workflow builds hardware first and then develops the control system, often using reinforcement learning. However, as seen in the agile locomotion of biological animals, morphology—such as limb lengths and joint compliance—and neural control are deeply intertwined. While morphology–control co-design optimizing both simultaneously has been studied theoretically, testing physical robots with freely variable link lengths and spring compliance faces severe fabrication constraints. As a result, most previous studies remained in narrow design spaces or simulation only.

To overcome this, the authors developed Dogger, a modular bio-inspired quadruped robot. Simply by swapping 3D-printed parts, one can reconfigure the lengths of its three leg segments (thigh, shank, and foot) as well as the stiffness and engagement offset of its parallel elastic actuators (PEA) at the knee. Furthermore, they devised a two-stage co-design framework: first, a morphology-conditioned universal control policy capable of handling diverse body shapes is pretrained with reinforcement learning; then, keeping that policy fixed, Bayesian optimization (BO) searches for the design that minimizes the cost of transport (CoT) for a specific task.

Using this framework, optimal morphologies were explored for two tasks: flat-ground inspection and payload-carrying. Distinct leg geometries and spring stiffnesses were selected for each task. When the optimized hardware was 3D-printed, assembled, and deployed on the physical robot, it achieved CoT reductions of 18.6% for inspection and 35.7% for payload-carrying compared to a standard springless design. This study clearly demonstrates at the hardware level the importance of simultaneously optimizing leg geometry and passive compliance.
contributions: Developed Dogger, a modular bio-inspired quadruped robot capable of rapid reconfiguration of three leg segment lengths (thigh, shank, foot) and parallel knee compliance (stiffness and engagement offset).

Proposed an efficient two-stage co-design method combining Bayesian optimization with a morphology-conditioned reinforcement learning policy that enables zero-shot physical deployment without additional retraining or policy distillation.
Demonstrated zero-shot sim-to-real transfer across inspection and payload-carrying tasks, achieving real-world cost of transport reductions of 18.6% and 35.7%, respectively.
Revealed through comparative experiments that full geometry–compliance co-design outperforms partial optimization of geometry alone or compliance alone in achieving the best energy efficiency.

sections.heading: Introduction: Why Co-design Body and Control for Legged Robots?
sections.summary: Biological creatures tightly integrate skeletal geometry, muscle-tendon compliance, and neural control to achieve highly efficient, agile movement. While quadruped robotics has traditionally focused on optimizing controllers for fixed hardware, morphology–control co-design is essential for true task-adapted efficiency. This work bridges that gap from design to hardware validation by combining reconfigurable modular hardware with reinforcement learning and Bayesian optimization.
sections.details:
Animal walking and running exhibit remarkable energy efficiency and robustness through the harmonious coordination of skeletal geometry, passive muscle-tendon compliance (parallel elastic actuators, or PEAs), and neural control systems. Recently, deep reinforcement learning (RL) has enabled quadruped robots to traverse rough terrain and execute acrobatic behaviors. However, most of these successes relied on training policies for fixed, preexisting hardware. When hardware dimensions or spring rates change, policies typically require retraining or tedious manual tuning.

Prior physical demonstrations, such as BirdBot mimicking avian leg mechanics or studies matching CPGs to passive elastic dynamics, have shown the critical importance of mechanism-control synergy. Algorithmically, simultaneous search over morphology and control (co-design) has also been explored using evolutionary algorithms, trajectory optimization, and meta-reinforcement learning. Yet real-world physical deployment has faced major bottlenecks: deciding which mechanical parameters can actually be swapped, prototyping and reconfiguring candidates quickly at low cost, and proving that simulated energy savings translate to physical hardware.

To address these challenges, this paper tackles the problem along three pillars:
- Developing Dogger, a modular quadruped robot featuring three-segment leg linkages and parallel knee compliance, allowing leg geometry and stiffness to be freely altered without changing the chassis, motors, or computing hardware.
- Building a two-stage framework consisting of a morphology-conditioned universal RL policy that controls varied body shapes with a single policy, paired with Bayesian optimization (BO) to discover task-specific designs.
- Achieving zero-shot transfer from simulation to hardware, experimentally measuring real-world CoT reductions of 18.6% for an inspection task and 35.7% for a payload-carrying task.

sections.heading: Methodology: Modular Leg Design and a Two-Stage Co-design Framework
sections.summary: The authors define a 5D design space specifying three leg link lengths and parallel knee compliance (stiffness and engagement offset). In the optimization pipeline, a single universal policy is first trained via reinforcement learning across an extensive design space, followed by Bayesian optimization selecting the design that minimizes task-specific cost of transport using that fixed policy. Sim-to-real transfer incorporates domain randomization, observation noise, feedforward torque compensation to cancel knee spring torques, and a comprehensive electrical power model.
sections.details:
The co-design approach consists of three key components: bio-inspired leg mechanisms, a two-stage optimization combining RL and Bayesian optimization, and a sim-to-real transfer strategy.

### II-A Bio-inspired Leg Design
Dogger's leg draws inspiration from animal anatomy, consisting of a three-segment linkage (thigh, shank, foot; four-bar parallel linkage) and a parallel spring (PEA) integrated into the knee joint. Leg parameters are defined by five variables: $\bm{d}=[\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3},\diameter,o]^{\text{T}}$. $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3$ scale the lengths of the thigh, shank, and foot from baseline values, ranging from 0.70 to 1.30. Parts can be produced on desktop 3D printers, allowing the entire leg unit to be swapped without removing a single motor.
The knee PEA extends a cable from an extension spring on the thigh ($c_s = 4180$ N/m) across a pulley at the knee joint to the shank. Altering the pulley diameter $\diameter$ (0 to 50 mm) tunes joint rotational stiffness between 0.03 and 2.62 Nm/rad. Sliding the clamp position $o$ (0 to 10 mm) along the cable adjusts the engagement angle where spring tension starts (initial torque from 0 to 5.62 Nm).

### II-B Two-Stage Optimization via RL and Bayesian Optimization
To avoid explosive computational costs, optimization is split into two steps:
- Step 1 (Universal Policy Learning): A single universal control policy $\pi_u$ is trained with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) across thousands of parallel simulation environments with designs $\bm{d}$ randomly sampled from the entire design space $\mathcal{D}$. Observations include robot velocity commands, joint angles, previous actions, and the design parameters $\bm{d}$ themselves. Free gait exploration is permitted without fixing foot trajectory motion primitives.
- Step 2 (Design Selection via Bayesian Optimization): For a given task $k$ (inspection or carrying), and with the trained policy $\pi_u$ held fixed, Bayesian optimization (Optuna's TPE) searches for the optimal design $\bm{d}^*_k$ that minimizes the cost of transport $CoT = E_{\text{total}} / (mg \Delta s)$. Although $CoT$ is non-differentiable with respect to design variables, BO's high sample efficiency identifies optimal designs rapidly.

### II-C Sim-to-Real Transfer
For zero-shot hardware deployment, the framework incorporates domain randomization of mass, inertia, and contact friction, alongside velocity disturbances and observation noise. In addition, feedforward torque compensation $\bm{\tau}^{\text{ff}}$ was introduced to cancel the passive torque generated by the knee spring. This relieves the policy from fighting extraneous spring torques, allowing it to focus on gait generation and energy utilization. A comprehensive power model accounting for motor winding copper losses ($\tau^2 R$), mechanical work, and baseline onboard electronics power ($P_{\text{system}}$) was also constructed to match simulated $CoT$ to physical power measurements.

captions.F1: Structure of Dogger's bio-inspired leg. Thigh, shank, and foot link lengths are adjusted via scaling factors ($\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \lambda_3$), rotational stiffness is tuned via the knee pulley diameter ($\diameter$), and spring engagement angle is set by the cable clamp position ($o$).
captions.F2: The proposed two-stage optimization pipeline. In simulation, a universal policy $\pi_u$ is trained via RL across diverse morphologies (Step 1). With $\pi_u$ fixed, Bayesian optimization selects the task-specific optimal design (Step 2). The physical robot executes zero-shot using the design parameters and spring feedforward compensation torques as inputs.

sections.heading: Results: Task-Specific Designs Validated on Real Hardware
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted on a flat-ground inspection task (Task 1) and an omnidirectional carrying task with a 2 kg payload (Task 2). In real-robot experiments, optimized designs reduced cost of transport by 18.6% and 35.7% compared to nominal baselines. Ablation experiments further demonstrated that co-designing both geometry and compliance simultaneously is essential for peak performance, while enabling robust locomotion on rough terrain without falling.
sections.details:
The experiments evaluated Task 1 (an inspection task alternating straight walking at 0.5 m/s and stationary holds on flat ground) and Task 2 (an omnidirectional transport task carrying a 2 kg weight—about 30% of robot body mass—across 16 velocity and heading commands over 2 minutes). Optimized designs $d^*_1$ and $d^*_2$ were compared against a springless nominal design $d^n_1$ and a medium-spring nominal design $d^n_2$.

### III-B Energy Savings from Task-Specific Co-design
- Task 1 (Inspection): The selected optimal design $d^*_1$ featured a short thigh, standard shank, and long foot ($\lambda_1=0.86, \lambda_2=1.02, \lambda_3=1.28$) with moderate stiffness ($\diameter=33$ mm, $o=6$ mm). In physical hardware tests, $d^*_1$ reduced $CoT$ by 18.6% ± 1.7% relative to the baseline design $d^n_1$. Knee motor torque profiles showed that the PEA significantly lowered peak torques and distributed them symmetrically around zero.
- Task 2 (Payload Carrying): The selected optimal design $d^*_2$ exhibited completely different proportions—a long thigh, extremely short shank, and long foot ($\lambda_1=1.30, \lambda_2=0.70, \lambda_3=1.30$)—with higher stiffness ($\diameter=38$ mm, $o=2$ mm). On the real robot, it achieved an impressive 35.7% ± 3.1% $CoT$ reduction over baseline $d^n_1$.
Because the study's $CoT$ calculation includes static electronics power (accounting for ~50% of total consumption), the reduction in pure motion-dependent energy expenditure is even more dramatic than the headline percentages suggest.

### III-C/D Cross-Task Validation and Partial Co-design Comparisons
Deploying $d^*_2$ on Task 1 yielded a 13.5% reduction, while running $d^*_1$ on Task 2 achieved a 23.7% reduction. While both beat the nominal design, neither matched the dedicated task-specific optimal design. This confirms the existence of purposeful, task-tailored optimal morphologies rather than a single universal shape.
In simulated ablations comparing partial optimization of link lengths only or springs only, spring compliance contributed more (7.3% reduction) than link lengths (1.1% reduction) in the inspection task. Conversely, link lengths contributed more (24.0% reduction) than spring compliance (16.3% reduction) in the payload task. Full co-design optimizing both simultaneously outperformed all alternatives (12.6% reduction for inspection, 34.0% for payload), highlighting the complementary interplay between geometry and compliance.

### III-E/F Baseline Comparisons and Outdoor Rough-Terrain Tests
Compared to prior methods such as CPG+CMA-ES and privileged RL+BO, the proposed method achieved the lowest $CoT$ on the carrying task, demonstrating strong competitiveness. Furthermore, when deployed on the real robot across harsh outdoor environments—gravel, tall grass, leaf-covered trails, and dirt slopes—the trained policy $\pi_u$ maintained stable locomotion for 17 minutes without a single reset or policy retuning.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook
sections.summary: Combining the modular Dogger platform with a two-stage co-design approach demonstrated on hardware that simultaneous optimization of geometry and passive compliance dramatically improves quadruped locomotion efficiency. Because the policy is fixed during the second stage, future work looks toward single-stage co-design updating policies and morphologies concurrently in the same loop, as well as incorporating broader structural constraints.
sections.details:
This paper realized purposeful morphology–control co-design using reinforcement learning and Bayesian optimization on Dogger, a bio-inspired quadruped featuring three-segment legs and adjustable knee compliance. By physically unlocking complementary design freedoms—geometric link lengths and passive elastic parameters—and pairing them with a morphology-conditioned policy, the authors successfully transferred simulated energy gains directly to physical hardware.

At the same time, the authors openly address limitations of the current two-stage framework. The design selection in Step 2 relies entirely on the fixed policy $\pi_u$ pretrained in Step 1. Consequently, if the policy fails to acquire proficient control skills for certain idiosyncratic morphologies, designs that might be mechanically superior could be prematurely dismissed.

To overcome this, evolving the framework into a single-stage (end-to-end) learned co-design where morphology and policy mutually adapt within the same learning loop represents a promising avenue. Furthermore, incorporating practical engineering limits—such as motor thermal limits and material strength—and extending the approach to continual learning frameworks that accumulate multi-task experience will serve as key milestones for automated robot development.

sections.heading: Appendix: Real-Robot Hardware Setup and Training Pipeline Details
sections.summary: Details of Dogger's electrical and mechanical design, simulation environments, and optimization hyperparameters are compiled here. The platform features a highly reproducible build leveraging low-cost commercial actuators (Xiaomi Cybergear) and FDM 3D-printed parts.
sections.details:
### Hardware Platform Specifications
Dogger was designed for low cost and high reproducibility using open-source and commercial off-the-shelf components.
- Dimensions and Weight: 37 cm length, 27 cm width, and a total weight of approximately 6.5 kg with nominal legs (sizing between a Unitree Go1 and an ODRI Solo 12).
- Structural Materials: Frame and leg links are fabricated on standard FDM 3D printers using conventional PLA, PETG, and TPU.
- Actuators and Power: Powered by twelve 24 V Xiaomi Cybergear actuators (12 Nm peak torque per joint). Power is supplied by a standard 2 Ah cordless drill lithium-ion battery via an MJbots power distribution board.
- Computing and Communication: An onboard NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano serves as the main computer. An M.2 PEAK CAN bus card (4 channels, one dedicated per leg) handles joint control and sensing at 50 Hz, communicating with an MPU-6050 IMU over I2C. Overall system power consumption is monitored in real time via a CANable 2.0 dongle.

### Training and Optimization Settings
- RL Training (Step 1): Flat-terrain tasks used the Brax environment (up to 8,192 parallel environments), while complex terrain tasks used NVIDIA Isaac Lab (4,096 parallel environments). Policy training takes between 15 minutes and 2 hours on a single desktop GPU (NVIDIA RTX 4070), depending on task complexity.
- Design Selection (Step 2): Using Optuna's TPE solver, optimization ran for 45 iterations with a batch size of 20 following 100 random sampling warm-up trials (1,000 evaluations total). This step took approximately 45 minutes on the same GPU.

takeaways: Simultaneously optimizing leg segment proportions and joint passive spring stiffness is an exceptionally powerful tool for robot energy reduction, extending far beyond control improvements alone.

The two-stage approach—pretraining a morphology-conditioned universal policy and then freezing it for Bayesian optimization over morphology—is highly practical and computationally efficient, eliminating retraining or distillation steps.

Optimal hardware morphologies differ drastically across tasks (flat inspection vs. payload transport); modular, reconfigurable mechanisms maximize overall system efficiency far better than a single general-purpose robot.
Incorporating feedforward torque compensation for knee springs and modeling baseline electronics power are subtle yet critical keys to high-fidelity sim-to-real transfer.
limitations: Design exploration in the second stage is bounded by the capabilities of the fixed policy trained in the first stage; morphologies the policy cannot control proficiently risk being unfairly penalized and discarded.
While modular leg swaps are straightforward, physical part replacement and spring clamp adjustments still require manual human intervention, falling short of full physical automation.
The design space is restricted to five parameters (three leg link lengths and two knee spring parameters), omitting torso dimensions, foot shapes, and ankle or hip passive compliance.
